item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I spent a good chunk of today reading this and I think I can answer some of the stuff on the inconsistencies:

+ show block
– hide block

There is not sufficient explanation for how the suffering on the moons produces the utopia on the planet, or how they are able to affect Earth's SCPs so greatly but yet not able to create something which can just transport humans about.

For the first part, the implication is that the suffering doesn't actually make things better for the people living in utopia, other than giving them a contrast so they can say "we aren't suffering like those sad sacks." Why they have decided it's so important is up to the reader's interpretation; personally I think that this society has concluded that human nature means humans can't be truly happy unless they know someone else isn'tbecause they're assholes. The second 990 log really gets that across to me.

As to the second part, I think that's due to whatever the original "fleeing" humans used to get away from this society, and I also think it's not perfect. As the second-to-last story shows, they can make doorways at least, and they can do other things to screw with reality. Not as much as they want, but enough to try and drive us back home.

There's no explanation for why making them think the planet is one large human worked to contain their influence

Quite simply, if you can't see your target clearly you'll have a devil of a time hitting it. Aside from making generic "screw with everything" SCPs and anomalies, blurring the lines between individual humans means they can't be targeted directly.

Or, indeed, during Threshold, any clarity on what did ultimately happen to either the people that went through the memorial or those who stayed behind.

The ones who went through the memorial "bought in" to the role of the suffering martyrs, which means they spent the rest of their lives suffering horribly for the sake of the people living in utopia. To start, that is; undoubtedly what happened is a lot worse than just you lose your hands and starve to death eventually, judging by the few "raw" glimpses we saw in other stories. As someone else pointed out, who knows how long they can prolong your life and your suffering.

Are the Children literally young people who migrate to a moon when they get old enough? Or was that metaphorical?

Definitely metaphorical. The Children are called that because (as per the second 990 log) they are the ones who live on without suffering while the "Parents" suffer and die to allow them to do so.

About the only thing I don't get is what effect the ending (and 2303) has on the whole mess, if anything. I think I'm missing something there.

item.title: Plaes halp Senpai
item.content:encoded:
I've read this entire canon, spin offs, and cross links like 8 times now…

Here's what I have:

Humans came to Earth because…?

With them came anomalies because human bodies are 4-dimensional expressions of higher dimensional (maybe our One Winged Angels use all 11 dimensions, plus the 15 implied by string theory) forms and all that junk data that got sheded when we dropped down causes reality to spaz out.

More anomalies are appearing nowadays because the gods (who are actually the children of ancient humans before we dropped down to 4 dimensions) just figured out how to contact 4th dimension humans and their interaction with lower space causes ripples. (Think the Flatland thought experiment on PCP)

This is where my understanding goes out the window.

So there's the 3 higher dimension planets, one for eyes, one for hands, one for skin, in addition to the standard, 3-dimensional Earth which is where 4-dimensional humans live. 1 quarter of the 4-dimensional humans will go to each world, with the remaining 25% staying in the third dimension.

Why can't we all go back to the higher worlds?

Why did we shed all but our lowest 4 dimensions to come to 3-dimensional Earth in the first place? What was so awesome on this mostly-blue rock that we considered mortality to be a fair trade?

Why did we leave our kids behind if this place was worth the trip?

What are the other 3 planets? You packed a whole bunch of symbolism that tells me they are central but I'm not smart enough to figure it out.

And what does the reverse-ghost-story at the end have to do with anything? Is it before 75% of humanity went back home or after? Also, if it's after, why are people choosing to stay here after death and not go home?

I feel like the money shot is in there somewhere. The story doesnt feel incomplete. It feels like its all there but I'm just too stupid to get it.

item.title: Fan Theories
item.content:encoded:
A place with endless light and nine orbiting bodies….without getting pedantic about Pluto, that sounds like the sun and solar system…

A future Dyson sphere civilization. With sufficiently advanced tech and all the power of a sun at their fingertips. They have solved immortality and want for nothing. But Malthus is always right eventually. So it is necessary to exile 9/10 to relatively hellish planet-bound colonies to maintain the sphere's high standard of living. Then we get Logan's Run. The suffering of exiles becomes something to be religiously exalted, seen as the direct fuel of societal perfection instead of a consequence of thermodynamics and human nature.
Eventually someone points out the logical conclusion. If suffering creates all we have, then more suffering would make it even better! So instead of just being sent to homestead on Mercury, the selected get a quick spoon-ing and off to The Moon of Eyes.

One colony managed to build up enough infrastructure and independent culture to not be cool with all this holy sacrifice for others. This is probably the moon formerly known as Earth, because that would be the least inherently lethal of all destinations. But how to escape a core society with practically infinite resources and fanatic zeal to chase you? Get clever and escape in a direction they can't go: time travel. Possibly using a skip found in some long-forgotten ruin of a containment chamber.

We are the descendants of those temporal refugees, with nothing but distorted tales from the oldest mythologies hinting at the truth. We think that the things in containment are monstrous and only occasionally realize in transient, small scale epiphanies that the worst nightmares are what mankind can (has and will) do to itself.

"Back home" the core society bends all resources to the mystery of what happened to the lost sheep. It is a holy crusade to bring the prodigals back to where they belong. A labor of true love by the honestly faithful to return everything to the way it should be. They don't have all the answers, but by scouring the Moon of Hands they found decrepit Foundation facilities and half-erased databases to create a connection. This conduit allowed certain energies and projections to be brought to bear. That would suffice. Especially given all they had learned about certain anomalies present in that by-gone era. Anomalies that could, with subtle energies directed by a certain man on the threshold between times, be influenced and adjusted to advance the holy cause of reunification.

If you can't tell, I liked this whole project so much that my brain immediately started trying to make more of it. Very well done, thank you.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I loved how this started, but soured on it about halfway through. The author is clearly a good storyteller — good with tone, good with mood — but there are aspects of the execution and of the story itself that just don't work for me.

I'll try to relate my thoughts on it, but this is from memory several days after reading. I've had time to digest it, but I can only really convey what I walked away with and not what I felt moment-to-moment.

This is a robbery! Gimme the hands and no one gets hurt!
I said show me your hands!

The SCP-001 documentation was good, but I think that's also where the proposal started to lose me a little bit. Ostensibly the anomaly's effect is to create anomalous phenomena to cause humanity distress, but not all of the SCP revisions seemed additionally distressing… to say nothing of how strange it is for the object to alter existing anomalies instead of just accelerating the production of new ones. (Yeah, come to think of it, the idea of the Foundation being unable to properly classify and study new anomalies, resorting to rush jobs, seems like it'd be interesting. Shame I'm not as good with prose as the author of this proposal; I might try it if I were.) The document started off as a good, original idea but then lost itself in out-of-place communications traffic and deliberately derivative takes on existing concepts.

Not too long after that, the proposal seemed to fall apart. Going from memory, it turned into abstract society-wide torture related allegorically, before apruptly ending with a document that I found incomprehensible. It may have been some kind of fight scene. And I think the end result of all this is that some of humanity lived, but now they don't have hands? Maybe? And the rest were just murder-tortured outright? I know I wasn't clear on either of those even at the time I read it.

I'm struggling to remember whether the story was unclear, overelaborate, or just too reliant on torture porn. Perhaps all three to some extent, but the more I think, the more I lean toward the latter.

Starting out, the threat is introduced to us without belaboring the point: it's a Very Uncool Dude and it's making lots of Very Uncool Things happen. After that, our primary information on the threat prior to "Hands Fall, Everyone Flies" comes from: a dream sequence whose primary focus is the physical torture of Dream Guy SCP and the emotional torture of an O5 (featuring a sexual assault mention that was understated, which is good in that it's not gratuitous, but it still didn't add anything); and another dream sequence, more or less, that isn't dissimilar. The point gets very much belabored, and if you lose your focus waiting for anything other than torture to happen (or even just waiting for more original torture), you get blindsided by the world getting tortured to death in a play and humanity maybe losing their hands.

There are SCP articles that show the end of the world, or the aftermath of another world's horrible end, without belaboring the point. I'm reminded of 3519 and the one with the planet of beetle lovers. Both of those are horrible ends, but we're shown just enough to know what's going on and then trusted to understand that they're horrible. 3519 knows we don't need to see, say, an apocalyptic cult crucifying a barely-a-character in graphic detail, to sell us on murder-suicides.

Which is to say: this proposal had very good prose, but I think that prose was misspent — the story was structured around wave after wave of torture. These ideas of humanity's secret past, of ancestors demanding our return by force, of other planets and strange cultures that can't quite relate to us (they think plays are normal informative broadcasts!), of our struggle to resist — these are all interesting, and they're all drowned out by ideas like, "Hey, wanna watch the Dream Guy scream in agony as he hangs from a cross?"

I +1'd the beginning parts and still wish I could +2 them, but overall, I give the proposal a -1. All in all, the writing style was good even if I think it went by too fast and leaned too heavily on the graphic and gratuitous. I don't really follow the site on a per-author basis, but I do hope I stumble across more writing from this one.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Reading through all of this has been a real experience. There are some things I have minor problems with (the lack of punctuation in dialogue), some things I struggled with (primarily understanding everything, and the vast number of cross-links), and one thing I have a serious ethical problem with (the casual dropped-in rape)… but overall, as a piece of literature, it achieved that ultimate accolade: disassociation. Only the best pieces of writing are sufficiently engaging to make the real world seem unreal afterwards, and this achieved that. So for that I must give the author an upvote.

However, I have some complaints. I didn't at all like the main -001 primarily because of its long list of spoilers for SCPs one may not yet have read and ultimately rather uninteresting effect. I did, however, like almost all of the tales, though each was not without its flaws.

My biggest concern is the lack of internal consistency with the story. There is not sufficient explanation for how the suffering on the moons produces the utopia on the planet, or how they are able to affect Earth's SCPs so greatly but yet not able to create something which can just transport humans about. There's no explanation for why making them think the planet is one large human worked to contain their influence (surely they'd realise something was up?) and there was not sufficient explanation for why they thought altering SCPs would be what would lead us back to them. Or, indeed, during Threshold, any clarity on what did ultimately happen to either the people that went through the memorial or those who stayed behind. Are the Children literally young people who migrate to a moon when they get old enough? Or was that metaphorical?

I understand that the author enjoys not revealing everything, but doing so runs the risk of merely appearing not entirely thought through, and it appears this has veered into that.

For all those caveats, I still thoroughly enjoyed spending the better part of my day reading this, and I am truly grateful for all the effort the author expended.

item.content:encoded:
The tie-ins are effective.

I made an account to comment on this article, so I guess that tells you something. It's one of my favorite SCP-001 proposals, although I do have some criticisms.

First, I don't think that an SCP should effectively end the world, without also restoring order after the fact. 2000 gets a pass, because that is literally its function. Especially given as 001 is ostensibly the first in a series, I don't think it's particularly appropriate for an 001 proposal to simultaneously spell the end of all things. The final .pdf story does a good job of humanizing the Foundation, but it is still too open-ended for an 001 proposalin my opinion.

Additionally, I feel that the presentation might be better served by collapsible links. I did find the current version somewhat cumbersome to read.

Finally, I would suggest that the presentation of the final story as part of the SCP's page is rather immersion breaking. Who recorded the story? Further, how did they know where to post it?

item.content:encoded:
I dunno, there's quite a few fate-worse-than-death SCPs out there, and it's less about the existing SCPs than it is about 001's ability to seemingly manifest whatever anomalies it wants to mess with us. Surely it could, and would, torture us forever. I mean that's its whole plan anyway. Also remember the suicide plan was concocted before anyone knew 001's motivation, back when to the best of their knowledge, it wanted only to use its seeming-omnipotence to cause us to suffer (which is actually correct, but not in the same way the Foundation was thinking).

Effective means of suicide, in this case, may be less about suicide definitely being better and more about just having the choice at all. Suicide, especially a relatively painless and dignified suicide, is not an easy thing to accomplish on one's own. A lot of people would go along with one of the less desirable routes out of a simple inability to do it themselves by any of the methods available to them.

returning to the system seems to offer a number of good years of life before an execution that's admittedly worse than the suicide pills.

Maaaaybe. Bear in mind, that's according to the play 001 put on for us, and probably won't apply to the people crossing the threshold. I do take issue with the idea that it's a execution they give; remember the handless woman had been suffering long enough to have forgotten entirely where she came from. I don't believe it's "starve for a few weeks and then die." We don't even know for sure that she died, and the people of this society are seemingly immortal; who knows HOW long they can prolong your suffering.

item.content:encoded:
I finished reading this, and it does make a surprisingly coherent and complete story (although it seems that 2798's dire warnings were all about 2798 and not about 001). I agree with the complaint that basically everything before the last two is mostly just foreshadowing, and that O5-2 isn't much of a character.

Assuming I'm understanding this correctly, it seems like the whole thing can be summarized as "Please come back to Omelas, child. You'll suffer either way (because we're sending bees after you), so why not do it for us?", which is fine, though it's been done before in one prominent way. This doesn't explain all SCPs — benevolent ones and ones that would threaten even 001 seem like a problem — but it doesn't really have to. I don't think the Children's reasoning quite makes sense, and you do rather gloss over why they've decided they need to go the Omelas route. It's also not clear why they'd make lethal demonstrations like with the dam; killing humans seems antithetical to their goals.

I'm not altogether sure why mass distribution of suicide pills is really better than 001 raging freely. Neither choice in this case seems worse than death. The amped-up anomalies mostly offer death (or, if you're lucky enough to be the president, REGOLITH SNAKES TO COMMAND), and returning to the system seems to offer a number of good years of life before an execution that's admittedly worse than the suicide pills. I guess giving people a third choice is good, but it doesn't feel clearly better than the other options.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I have thoroughly mixed feelings on this one.

+ show block
– hide block

I should say first that I don't have a set of criteria by which I judge 001 proposals. What I express here probably isn't how I objectively view 001s, it's just how it played out here.

I just don't buy it as the story of the Foundation, Foundation-verse, or origin of all SCPs. This feels like an essentially unrelated story told through the Foundation-verse. I mentioned that in a sub-article and it contributed to my upvoting of that article, but as it applies to the whole story it really doesn't do much for me.

I think the story of the society of the five moons and the rogue planet was interesting. The irony of O5-2's reading of the omens as something worth aspiring to, and getting exactly what she wanted in the most horrible way, was excellently done. But it just doesn't feel integrated at all, even remotely. Again, this is not a story of the Foundation or their world. You tell it through SCPs and the Foundations voices and actions, but from their perspective, it could just as easily have been a Great Old One or YHWH. From the perspective of the alien's story, this might as well have been generals talking back and forth in the Pentagon. It would've had to have been told differently, sure, but that doesn't mean they're narratively related.

If there were more about the secret past escape, and how our science and anomalies were influenced or created by their influence, and that tied in with past SCPs, I'd probably be more comfortable with it. I understand that that's incidental to the story, and that the story itself doesn't need any more than what was presented, but I see it as a missed opportunity.

As for the story of the society itself… it's balanced and whole, but that doesn't mean I like it. The high-handed philosophizing perfect society represented is well described, but the idea is cold and distant. It's like a well thought-out proof, but the answer (I guess I mean ending) doesn't satisfy me. They're this balanced hell-society living in perfect order together, and at least some of us just go back to them, as is probably inevitable given that they've conquered all of creation and science and created perfect eternal balance and it must be that way, Q.E.D..

I admit I like happy endings. It's a bias. That, or at least hopeful, or at least interesting endings, with potential for change. This is way too clean and self-aggrandizing. This Eschaton of the Foundation-verse sucks itself into an unforshadoewed, unrelated-feeling story, blows the whole thing up, and locks what's left to that hell-scape forever. That narrative didn't grab me beyond the tense anticipation of further revelations, and now that all is known, I just don't care.

So, I think… no vote on the overall story, leaning to down. I've upvoted or no-voted individual pages and will leave them as such.

item.title: No vote because of the page's format
item.content:encoded:
While I have upvoted the articles linked from this page, I will not vote on this page. I agree with some of the criticisms in earlier comments on how the proposal is presented. I think the collective story linked from this page is amazingly compelling and certainly deserves a place in the SCP-001 proposals, but I feel that the format of this hub should be presented in a different way.

Here is my suggestion for a new format.
The SCP-001 file itself, Night at the Movies, and the Standard Dream Reports should be moved onto this page, perhaps kept under javascript tags. Harbinger, After Action Report, and The Man at the Threshold are fine as they are, since they all are relatively long stories, and are written as tales. They belong on separate pages from this one.

Changing the format to something like this would make the page feel closer to a legitimate SCP-001 proposal rather than just a short blurb and some links.

item.title: In Conclusion
item.content:encoded:
And so it ends. A story beyind the traditional scope of time, of epic secrets hidden and coming to light, of reality breaking apart and forging itself anew, of our newborne Father coming to save its parents in an engrossing, vivid and thickly made story.

I give it a -1.

 "Wait, what?" 
Lemme explain

Because, although the characterization is splendid and the prose imaginative (Man at the Threshold; told as a Play for it is a performance told across the planet—clever!), I have one very keen problem with this… It goes fucking nowhere. SCP-001 has been unleashed. What happens?

A couple SCPs act a bit weird in new ways, people lose their hands, China has a new government, we lost an O5 and some people are leaving Earth to the "Planet of Hands", whatever the fuck that is. It just feels all so lacklustre. Like, this is the End of Days, something which will induce Great, Worldwide suffering as a certain Dream foretold—and the most sudden changes we see on a global scale is a) some riots and murdere, b) people realise "Oh, so science is wrong, huh" and then they just fuck off into the OMINOUS Washington Monument.

And I'm sitting here going, "OH MAN, WHERE WILL THIS STORY GO!? THE FOUNDATION HAS BEEN REVEALED, NORMALITY IS NON-EXISTENT—NEXT STORY!"

And then I'm told "Yeah, that it, show over kids". And that just rubs me the wrong way. Because this is a story that had all of the fucking buildup and hype—twice. We had a Mainlist SCP that foretold it, and then the Hub was revealed to be a series of Tales that would be updated bit by bit to weave an epic tapestry. And when it's done, all we get is "We must go, our planet needs us" and it's over. All of this, and the biggest change is there's less people on Earth by a certain unknown degree (3000 of 50'000 went into Washington, so I'm getting the impression of "not many people give a shit to leave") and China is under new management.

That is just irrevocably boring way to finish this, and it saddens me.


So yeah. It was a nice story in all accounts, but with that lacklustre ending, the completely unnecessary buildup (I see no Narrative Purpose for this to have been told over the course of multiple days), the things left unanswered and vague, and the completely underwhelming nature of the -001 in general, this has my personal disapproval.

But hey, don't let my opinion wear ya down. This is still nicely done by most accounts, and what the hell is my opinion worth? I haven't even made one SCP.
